info.title: FixFlow Manufacturer API
info.description:
The **FixFlow Manufacturer API** is the machine surface of a manufacturer's own systems
(warranty desk, CRM, reporting). It is authenticated by an API key, versioned in the path, and
documented by this single artefact: the document you are reading **is** the contract.

This is release **1.0.0**, the first released version of `v1`. The endpoints listed below are its
whole surface; later releases only add to it and record every change in the
[Changelog](#changelog).

## Getting started

Three words are used throughout: a **site** is one service location of one of your end customers, a
**unit** is one installed piece of your equipment, and a **work order** is the repair request FixFlow
tracks (your own system may call it a claim or a case).

The whole integration is five steps, in this order:

1. **Get a key** and store it — [Getting a key](#getting-a-key). It goes into the `X-Api-Key` header
   of every call ([Authentication](#authentication)).
2. **Verify the key**: `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/key` answers with the manufacturer your key is
   bound to. If this call works, everything below is reachable.
3. **Register your directory** — [Registering your directory](#registering-your-directory):
   `POST /customers` per end customer, `POST /service-locations` per site of that customer,
   `POST /equipment` per installed unit. Each one is addressed by **your own** key and is idempotent
   on it, so re-registering everything nightly is safe and cheap.
4. **Create work orders with keys only** — [Creating a work order](#creating-a-work-order):
   `POST /work-orders` with `externalReference`, `customer.reference`, `serviceLocation.reference`,
   the unit's `serialNumber`, a `description`, and optionally a `problemId` from the
   [problem catalog](#problem-catalog). Because the keys are already registered, the work order
   needs nothing else — see [Which fields are needed when](#which-fields-are-needed-when).
5. **Poll the feed** — [Tracking status](#tracking-status): subscribe once to
   `GET /work-orders/changes`, store the cursor it returns, then poll every 30–60 seconds and apply
   the snapshots you get.

Steps 3 and 4 can be mixed in any order: a work order for a key we have never seen registers that
key on the way, and then it also has to carry the customer's name and the site's address.
Registering up front simply means every work order is "keys only" from the very first one.

## Base URL

Every path in this document is relative to the API base of your FixFlow deployment:

```
https://<your-fixflow-host>/fixflow
```

So the verify-key call below is `GET https://<your-fixflow-host>/fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/key`.
Your FixFlow contact gives you the host; the `/fixflow` segment is part of the base and does not
change.

## Getting a key

Use one key per integrating system, never one per person. There are two ways to get one:

- **Self-service**: sign in to the FixFlow manufacturer portal and open **API keys**. Any active
  user of your company can create and revoke your company's keys there.
- **Through FixFlow staff**: ask your FixFlow contact, naming the system that will use the key
  (for example `Warranty desk`).

Either way:

1. The full key value is shown **once**, at creation time, and is never retrievable again. Store it
   in your secret manager immediately.
2. Call `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/key` to confirm the key works and to see which manufacturer it is
   bound to.

A key can be revoked at any time; a revoked key is rejected from the next request on. To rotate,
create a new key, deploy it, then revoke the old one. Several keys can be active at once, so
rotation needs no downtime.

## Authentication

Send the key in the `X-Api-Key` request header on **every** call:

```http
GET /fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/key HTTP/1.1
Host: <your-fixflow-host>
X-Api-Key: ffmfr_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
```

Rules that will not change within `v1`:

- `X-Api-Key` is the only accepted credential. A bearer token (JWT) from the FixFlow web portals is
  **not** accepted here, and a Manufacturer API key is **not** accepted outside
  `/manufacturer-api/v1/*`.
- The manufacturer is taken from the key alone. There is no `manufacturerId` parameter to pass, and
  no way to read another manufacturer's data with your key — rows that are not yours do not exist
  for the API.
- Always use HTTPS. A key sent over plain HTTP must be treated as leaked and revoked.

## Demo client

A small MIT-licensed reference client (Node.js, TypeScript) shows the whole integration end to end:

- verifying the key;
- creating work orders with safe retries;
- the polling loop over the change feed with a stored cursor;
- handling `429`.

It runs against a built-in mock of this API, so you can try it before you have a key. Once you
give it your base URL and a key, it works against your FixFlow deployment. The key stays on the
client's server and never reaches a browser.

**Repository:** coming soon. The public link will be published here.

## Registering your directory

You can register your end customers, their sites and your installed units **before** you ever send a
work order, instead of letting the first work order create them. Either way works — and you can mix
them — but registering up front means the keys are already known by the time a work order arrives,
so the work order itself needs nothing but those keys.

| Call | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /manufacturer-api/v1/customers` | Registers an end customer under your own `reference` |
| `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/customers/{reference}` | Reads that customer back |
| `POST /manufacturer-api/v1/service-locations` | Registers one of that customer's sites under your own `reference` |
| `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/service-locations/{reference}` | Reads that site back |
| `POST /manufacturer-api/v1/equipment` | Registers one of your units at that site, keyed by its serial number |
| `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/equipment?serialNumber=…` | Looks your units up by serial number |

The directory belongs to the service company, so registration only ever **finds or creates** a row:

- it **never updates or deletes** anything — a name or address you send for a row we already have is
  ignored, and corrections go to your FixFlow contact;
- there is no `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`, and no listing: a registered row is read back one key at a
  time.

### Idempotency

`reference` is the idempotency key, exactly as `externalReference` is for a work order:

- the first call with a given value answers `201 Created` with a `Location` header — both when a new
  row was created and when an existing one was found;
- every later call with the same value answers `200 OK` with the **same, unchanged** row and the
  response header `Idempotent-Replayed: true`. The body of a repeat is ignored entirely;
- two calls that race each other still produce exactly one row and one mapping.

So retrying a timed-out registration is always safe, and a nightly "register everything again" job
costs nothing but requests.

### Registering a customer

```http
POST /fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/customers HTTP/1.1
X-Api-Key: ffmfr_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "reference": "CUST-99812",
  "name": "Riverside Dental",
  "address": {
    "addressLine1": "125 West State Street",
    "addressLine2": "Suite 3",
    "city": "Trenton",
    "state": "NJ",
    "zip": "08608"
  },
  "phone": "+1 609 555 0142"
}
```

```json
{ "id": 318, "reference": "CUST-99812", "name": "Riverside Dental" }
```

`reference` and `name` are required. `address` is optional, but if you send it, `addressLine1`,
`city`, `state` and `zip` are all required — and it is what makes matching possible:

- **with `address`** we look for a customer with the same name **and** the same `addressLine1` + ZIP,
  either as the customer's own address or as the address of one of its sites, and map your key onto
  it; otherwise a new customer is created from what you sent;
- **without `address`** nothing is matched and a new customer is always created. A name alone is
  never enough: two unrelated companies may share one.

So send the address whenever you have it — that is how your key lands on a customer a dispatcher or
another manufacturer already created, instead of a duplicate.

### Registering a service location

```http
POST /fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/service-locations HTTP/1.1
X-Api-Key: ffmfr_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "reference": "SITE-4471",
  "customerReference": "CUST-99812",
  "name": "Trenton clinic",
  "addressLine1": "125 West State Street",
  "addressLine2": "Suite 3",
  "city": "Trenton",
  "state": "NJ",
  "zip": "08608",
  "phone": "+1 609 555 0150"
}
```

```json
{
  "id": 904,
  "reference": "SITE-4471",
  "customer": { "id": 318, "reference": "CUST-99812", "name": "Riverside Dental" },
  "name": "Trenton clinic",
  "addressLine1": "125 West State Street",
  "addressLine2": "Suite 3",
  "city": "Trenton",
  "state": "NJ",
  "zip": "08608"
}
```

`reference` is your own id for the site, up to 100 characters; if your system has no such id, see
[No site id in your system?](#the-two-keys-you-must-send) — it is the same key the work-order call
takes. `customerReference` must be a customer **you** have already registered, otherwise the call
answers `422` on that field — register the customer first. The address is always required here, because it is
what the site is matched by: among that customer's existing sites we look for the same
`addressLine1` + ZIP and map your key onto it, otherwise the site is created and named `name` (or,
if you omit it, after the street line).

### Registering a unit

```http
POST /fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/equipment HTTP/1.1
X-Api-Key: ffmfr_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "serviceLocationReference": "SITE-4471",
  "serialNumber": "SN-77421",
  "modelNumber": "AC-200",
  "name": "Rooftop unit A"
}
```

```json
{
  "id": 7741,
  "serialNumber": "SN-77421",
  "modelNumber": "AC-200",
  "name": "Rooftop unit A",
  "serviceLocation": { "id": 904, "reference": "SITE-4471" }
}
```

A unit has no key of yours: its key is its **serial number**, among the units of your own brand. So
`serialNumber` is required here, and so is `modelNumber` — a unit that is created needs at least one
way to say what it is. `serviceLocationReference` must be a site **you** have already registered,
otherwise the call answers `422` on that field. `name` is what a dispatcher sees in lists; omit it and
the model number is used.

The serial number is the idempotency key, together with the site:

- no unit of yours carries it yet → the unit is created under your brand → `201 Created` with a
  `Location` header pointing at the lookup below;
- one of your units **at that same site** already carries it → `200 OK` with the same, unchanged unit
  and `Idempotent-Replayed: true`;
- one of your units **at a different site** carries it → `409 Conflict`, and nothing is changed. We
  never move a unit between sites: if the equipment really was relocated, ask the dispatcher.

Unlike customers and sites, two **parallel** registrations of one new serial number may create two
units — there is no database-level guard on a serial number. Repeats one after another are safe, so
register serially (or just retry on failure) and a duplicate stays an edge case a dispatcher can
merge.

If `modelNumber` is in your model catalogue in FixFlow the unit is linked to that model; an unknown
model number is kept as free text, so nothing is rejected over it.

Matching only ever looks at units of **your** brand: equipment of another brand is never matched,
changed or reported, even when it carries the very same serial number. A unit created this way is
visible to you in every work-order read, exactly like one created by a work order.

### Looking a unit up

```http
GET /fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/equipment?serialNumber=SN-77421 HTTP/1.1
X-Api-Key: ffmfr_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
```

```json
{
  "items": [
    {
      "id": 7741,
      "serialNumber": "SN-77421",
      "modelNumber": "AC-200",
      "name": "Rooftop unit A",
      "serviceLocation": { "id": 904, "reference": "SITE-4471" }
    }
  ]
}
```

`serialNumber` is required (`422` otherwise). The answer is a list because historical duplicates can
exist in the directory; normally there is exactly one item, and an unknown serial number is an empty
`items` rather than a `404`. Comparison ignores letter case and extra spaces, and the scope is your
own brand only. `serviceLocation.reference` is your key for that site, or `null` if you never
registered one for it — which is what you see for a unit a work order or a dispatcher created.

There is no update, no delete and no read by FixFlow id for units either.

### Reading a registration back

The customer and site reads are addressed by **your** key and scoped to it: a reference you never
registered, and the same value registered by another manufacturer, both answer the same `404`. The
resources are deliberately minimal — phone, email and the customer's own address stay inside FixFlow.
`customer.reference` on a site is your key for that customer, or `null` if you never registered one.

## Creating a work order

`POST /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders` submits a repair request for one of your units at an end
customer's site. You do not need to know any FixFlow identifier: you address the customer and the
site with **your own keys**, and FixFlow matches them against its own directories or creates the
missing rows. The work order opens in status `New` and a dispatcher takes it from there; you do not
choose the service company.

The response is the **work-order resource** — the same shape every read returns.

### The two keys you must send

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `customer.reference` | the end customer's id in **your** system |
| `serviceLocation.reference` | the site's id in **your** system |

Both are required, both are strings of up to 100 characters, and both are scoped to your key: the
same value used by another manufacturer points at something else entirely and is never read or
changed by your calls.

Send them consistently and every later work order for that site lands on the same customer and the
same site in FixFlow — an address written differently the second time no longer creates a duplicate.

**No site id in your system?** Use any key you can rebuild from your own data for the same site
every time — for example the customer id plus the site number (`CUST-99812/4`), the id of the
installation record, or (when a customer has exactly one site) the customer id with a fixed suffix.
It never has to mean anything to FixFlow; it only has to be stable, unique among your sites and no
longer than 100 characters. The same answer applies to
`serviceLocation.reference` in [Registering a service location](#registering-a-service-location) —
there is one kind of site key, used by both calls.

### Which fields are needed when

Resolution is **key first, then data**. A key we have already seen leads straight to its directory
row, so everything that would otherwise be used to find that row becomes unnecessary — and is
ignored if you send it anyway. We never overwrite a stored customer or site from a request.

This table is the **one place** the conditional fields are stated; the sections below only explain
how each row is matched.

| Field | Needed |
| --- | --- |
| `externalReference` | **always** — it is the idempotency key of the call |
| `customer.reference`, `serviceLocation.reference` | **always** — your own keys, up to 100 characters |
| `description` | **always** — it is what the dispatcher reads first |
| `customer.name` | only while `customer.reference` is still unknown to us |
| `serviceLocation.addressLine1`, `.city`, `.state`, `.zip` | only while `serviceLocation.reference` is still unknown to us |
| `equipment.modelNumber` | only when no unit of yours with that `serialNumber` is found at the site |
| `equipment.serialNumber` | never required, but it is what identifies the unit — send it whenever you have it |
| `problemId` | never — it is optional (see [Problem catalog](#problem-catalog)) |
| `urgency`, `deadline`, `isWarranty`, `warrantyReference`, `purchaseOrder`, `serviceLocation.name`, `serviceLocation.addressLine2`, `serviceLocation.phone`, `customer.phone`, `customer.email`, `equipment.name`, `onSiteContact` | never — all optional detail |

The schema marks as required only what is required **always**, so the simplest way to work is to
keep sending the full body: the first work order for a customer or site registers the key, and later
ones may send the keys alone. A field that is needed and missing answers `422` naming that very
field, so nothing is ever silently guessed.

A key you registered in advance (see [Registering your directory](#registering-your-directory)) is
already known, so a work order for it can carry **nothing but the keys** — no customer name, no
address:

```json
{
  "externalReference": "CLM-2026-55120",
  "customer": { "reference": "CUST-99812" },
  "serviceLocation": { "reference": "SITE-4471" },
  "equipment": { "modelNumber": "AC-200", "serialNumber": "SN-77421" },
  "description": "Unit shuts down after 10 minutes and reports error E-14."
}
```

### Idempotency

`externalReference` is your own claim or case number and is **required**. It is the idempotency key,
unique per manufacturer:

- the first call with a given value creates the work order and answers `201 Created` with a
  `Location` header;
- every later call with the same value answers `200 OK` with that **same, unchanged** work order and
  the response header `Idempotent-Replayed: true`;
- two calls that race each other still produce exactly one work order.

So retrying a request that timed out is always safe, and you never need a "did it get through?"
lookup before retrying. The replay never changes anything: send corrected data under a **new**
`externalReference`, or ask the dispatcher.

### How the customer is matched

The customer of the work order is the **end customer** whose unit is broken — not you.

1. If `customer.reference` is one we have already seen, that customer is used — even if the name or
   address in this request differs.
2. Otherwise `customer.name` is required, and we look for a customer with the same name **and** a
   site at the same `addressLine1` + ZIP. Name alone is never enough: two unrelated companies may
   share a name. If you sent a site key we already know, the address of that site is used for this
   step, and any address in the request is ignored.
3. Otherwise a new customer is created.

In cases 2 and 3 your `customer.reference` is remembered and points at that customer from then on.

### How the service location is matched

1. If `serviceLocation.reference` is one we have already seen, that site is used and the address in
   the request is ignored. The site must belong to the customer resolved above — a site of a
   different customer answers `422` on `serviceLocation.reference`, because a work order must not
   land on someone else's site. So does a site that has since been deactivated in FixFlow: send a new
   site key for it.
2. Otherwise the full address is required, and among that customer's sites we look for the same
   `addressLine1` + ZIP, otherwise we create the site (named `serviceLocation.name`, or the street
   line if you omit it). Your `serviceLocation.reference` is remembered and points at that site from
   then on.

ZIP matching uses the first five digits, so `08608` and `08608-1234` are the same place. Comparisons
ignore letter case and extra spaces.

The resource echoes your key back as `serviceLocation.reference`, so a read tells you which of your
sites a work order belongs to without storing FixFlow ids.

### How the unit is matched

The unit always belongs to the manufacturer your key is bound to. Matching only ever looks at your
own units at that site — equipment of another brand is never matched and never modified, even if it
carries the same serial number or model.

- With `equipment.serialNumber` we match on the serial number; a unit found that way needs no
  `equipment.modelNumber`.
- Without a serial number we match on `equipment.modelNumber`, but only if there is exactly one such
  unit at the site. Several identical models, or none, means there is nothing to match safely.
- Otherwise a new unit is created under your brand, and `equipment.modelNumber` is required for it
  (`422` otherwise).

If the model number is in your model catalogue in FixFlow the unit is linked to that model; an
unknown model number is kept as free text, so nothing is rejected over it.

A unit you registered in advance (see [Registering your directory](#registering-your-directory)) is
found by its serial number alone. Note that work-order create is deliberately more lenient than
registration here: a serial number known at **another** site creates a new unit at the site of the
work order instead of answering `409`, because a service request matters more than a tidy directory.

### Naming the fault

`description` is free text and always required — it is what the dispatcher reads first
(see [Which fields are needed when](#which-fields-are-needed-when)). On top of it you may send
`problemId`, the id of an entry in our [problem catalog](#problem-catalog), so the fault is also
classified the same way our own dispatchers classify it.

- It is optional. Without it the work order simply arrives unclassified and a dispatcher assigns a
  problem on triage.
- An id that is not in the catalogue answers `422` on `problemId`; we never silently drop it.
- We do not check that the problem suits the unit's equipment type — a plausible mismatch is a
  dispatcher's call, not a reason to reject a service request.
- The dispatcher may change the problem later. The work-order resource always shows the current one
  as `problem { id, name }` (or `null`), and the change reaches you through the change feed.

### Validation

A body that fails validation answers `422` with `errors` keyed by the JSON path of the field, for
example `customer.reference` or `serviceLocation.zip`. Problems are reported in groups, all entries
of a group at once: first the structural ones (a missing key, a value that is too long, a malformed
`urgency` or `deadline`), then — once your keys have been looked up — the fields this particular
request still needs. Unknown fields in the body are ignored.

## Tracking status

There are no webhooks in `v1`. You poll, and we make polling cheap: the **change feed** tells you
which of your work orders moved, so you never re-read the ones that did not.

The three reads all return the same work-order resource, and all of them see the same scope — every
work order whose unit is one of your brand's, not only the ones you created through this API,
**including archived ones** (they come back with `archivedAt` set, so archiving reads as a state and
not as a disappearance):

| Call | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/changes` | The normal loop: what changed since last time |
| `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders?ids=…&references=…` | Resync: re-read up to 100 at once |
| `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/{id}` and `/by-reference/{externalReference}` | One work order, on demand |

### The polling loop

1. **Subscribe.** Call `changes` once with no parameters. You get `items: []` and a `nextCursor`
   that means "from now on". Store that cursor where it survives a restart.
2. **Poll.** Every **30–60 seconds** call `changes?cursor=<stored cursor>`. Apply the `items`, then
   store the new `nextCursor` — ideally in the same transaction, so a crash cannot lose it.
3. **Drain.** While the answer says `hasMore: true`, more changes are already waiting: call again
   right away with the cursor you just stored instead of waiting for the next tick.
4. **Resync** if you ever lose the cursor or suspect your copy is stale: read the work orders you
   care about with the batch call, then subscribe again.

```http
GET /fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/changes?cursor=djE6ODgxNDI&limit=100 HTTP/1.1
X-Api-Key: ffmfr_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
```

```json
{
  "items": [
    { "id": 10427, "status": "Done", "changedAt": "2026-10-13T15:48:02Z" }
  ],
  "nextCursor": "djE6ODgxNTA",
  "hasMore": false
}
```

(`items` entries are full work-order resources; the one above is abridged.)

### Rules of the feed

- **Items are snapshots, not events.** Each item is the work order exactly as it is now, plus
  `changedAt` — when we last saw it change. Several changes to one work order inside one page
  collapse into a single item, and the feed never tells you which field moved.
- **Delivery is at-least-once, so be idempotent.** The same snapshot can arrive twice — after a
  retry, or simply because you reused a cursor. Apply items by `id` (upsert), never by counting
  them.
- **The cursor is opaque.** Store the string verbatim; do not parse it, order it or build one
  yourself. An invalid cursor answers `422`, and the fix is a resync, not a retry.
- **A moved cursor with an empty page is normal.** Changes to work orders outside your scope move
  the cursor without being shown.
- **The feed lags a few seconds behind live** by design, so that a change committed slightly out of
  order is never skipped. Status changes therefore reach you a few seconds after they happen.
- `limit` is 1–500, 100 by default. `since=<ISO-8601 instant>` starts from a moment instead of
  subscribing from now; `cursor` wins when you send both.

Changes to any of these resource fields put a work order on the feed: `status` (and with it the
stage timestamps and `completedAt`), `urgency`, `description`, `deadline`, `isWarranty`,
`warrantyNumber`, `scheduledServiceAt`, the unit, the `problem`, and `archivedAt`.

A work order that leaves your scope — a dispatcher relinks the unit to another brand — stops being
readable (`404` / `notFound`) and does **not** produce a feed item.

### Reading a batch

`ids` and `references` take comma-separated lists and may be mixed, up to **100 identifiers in
total**; more answers `422`. Unknown identifiers, another manufacturer's, and work orders no longer
in your scope all come back under `notFound`, echoed exactly as you sent them — one bad identifier
never fails the whole call.

```json
{
  "items": [],
  "notFound": { "ids": [99999], "references": ["CLM-UNKNOWN"] }
}
```

## Problem catalog

`GET /manufacturer-api/v1/problems` returns the catalogue of problem codes our dispatchers use, so
you can classify a fault with `problemId` (see [Naming the fault](#naming-the-fault)) instead of
describing it in free text only.

The catalogue belongs to the service company. It is read-only through this API — there is no way to
add, change or remove an entry — and it is **not** manufacturer-specific: every key sees the same
entries. Internal accounting attributes (estimates, DNE limits, GL codes, CapEx and deferral flags)
are never part of the response.

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | what you send as `problemId` |
| `name` | the problem as a dispatcher reads it |
| `code` | our catalogue code, or `null` |
| `description` | a longer explanation, or `null` |
| `equipmentType` | the equipment type this problem belongs to, by name, or `null` |

```http
GET /fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/problems?equipmentType=HVAC&limit=100 HTTP/1.1
X-Api-Key: ffmfr_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
```

```json
{
  "items": [
    {
      "id": 412,
      "name": "Unit does not cool",
      "code": "HVAC-COOL",
      "description": "No cooling at all, or the discharge air stays above setpoint.",
      "equipmentType": "HVAC"
    }
  ],
  "nextCursor": "cDE6NDEy",
  "hasMore": true
}
```

- **Paging** works like the change feed: `limit` is 1–500 (100 by default), and while `hasMore` is
  `true` you call again with `cursor` set to the `nextCursor` you just received. On the last page
  `nextCursor` is `null`. The cursor is opaque — store it verbatim, and do not reuse a cursor from
  the change feed here (it answers `422`).
- **Filters.** `equipmentType` keeps the problems of one equipment type, matched on the type's exact
  name, case-insensitively. `search` keeps the problems whose name or code contains the text you
  pass, case-insensitively. Both may be combined.
- The catalogue changes rarely, so the usual pattern is to walk it once, cache it on your side and
  refresh it on a schedule — not on every work order.

## Errors

Every error response is a [`ProblemDetails`](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457) body with the
content type `application/problem+json`:

```json
{
  "title": "Unauthorized",
  "detail": "A valid API key is required.",
  "status": 401
}
```

| Status | When | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `401 Unauthorized` | The `X-Api-Key` header is missing, empty, unknown or revoked — or a JWT was sent instead of a key. | Fix the credential. Do not retry with the same key. |
| `404 Not Found` | The addressed resource does not exist **or** belongs to another manufacturer — the two cases are deliberately indistinguishable. | Check the identifier; do not treat it as "exists but forbidden". |
| `422 Unprocessable Entity` | The request body or query failed validation. `errors` carries the per-field messages. | Fix the payload; retrying unchanged will fail again. |
| `429 Too Many Requests` | The per-key rate limit is exhausted. | Wait `Retry-After` seconds, then retry. |
| `400 Bad Request` | The request could not be parsed or bound at all (malformed JSON, wrong parameter type). | Fix the request. |
| `409 Conflict` | A write collided with the current state of the data. | Re-read the resource and decide. |

`5xx` responses are our fault. They are safe to retry with backoff for idempotent requests
(`GET`); report them if they persist.

## Rate limits

Requests are counted **per key** in a one-minute sliding window; the default allowance is **120
requests per minute**. Over the limit the API answers `429` with a `Retry-After` header in seconds
and no side effects. The limit protects the shared service, so poll on a schedule rather than in a
tight loop, and keep one key per system so one noisy job cannot starve another.

## Versioning policy

The major version lives in the path (`/manufacturer-api/v1/...`) and `info.version` carries the
published document version.

Within `v1` we only make **additive** changes, and your client must tolerate them:

- new endpoints, new optional request fields, new response fields;
- new values in an existing enumeration;
- new `4xx` reasons for input we already rejected.

A **breaking** change — removing or renaming a path, operation, parameter or response field,
narrowing a type, dropping an enumeration value, or making an existing input required — is never
shipped inside `v1`. It goes to `/manufacturer-api/v2`, which is announced before it is released and
runs alongside `v1`.

This is enforced on our side, not promised in prose: release `1.0.0` of this document is frozen as a
compatibility baseline, and our build compares every later document against it. A change that
removes or narrows anything, or makes an input required, fails the build before it can be released.

Practical client rules: ignore unknown response fields, treat unknown enumeration values as
"unmapped" instead of failing, and never depend on property order or on the exact wording of
`title`/`detail`.

## Changelog

### 1.0.0 — 2026-10-11 — initial release

The first released version of the contract, and the compatibility baseline of `v1`. Its whole
surface:

- **Authentication and limits** — `X-Api-Key` on every call, `ProblemDetails` errors, a per-key rate
  limit answering `429` with `Retry-After`; see [Authentication](#authentication),
  [Errors](#errors) and [Rate limits](#rate-limits).
- `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/key` — verify a key and read the manufacturer it is bound to.
- `POST /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders` — create a work order. `externalReference`,
  `customer.reference`, `serviceLocation.reference` and `description` are required; `problemId` is
  optional and classifies the fault from the problem catalogue. Resolution is key first, then data,
  so a registered key needs nothing else (see
  [Which fields are needed when](#which-fields-are-needed-when)). Idempotent on
  `externalReference`: a repeat answers `200` with the same, unchanged work order and
  `Idempotent-Replayed: true`.
- `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/{id}` and
  `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/by-reference/{externalReference}` — read one work order;
  unknown, another manufacturer's and out-of-scope all answer `404`.
- `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders?ids=…&references=…` — read up to 100 at once →
  `{ items, notFound }`.
- `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/changes` — the change feed with an opaque cursor →
  `{ items, nextCursor, hasMore }`; see [Tracking status](#tracking-status). Items are full
  work-order resources, so each one carries `problem` and `serviceLocation.reference`; a problem
  changed by a dispatcher puts the work order on the feed, exactly like a status change.
- Reads see archived work orders too (`archivedAt` is set on them).
- `POST /manufacturer-api/v1/customers` and `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/customers/{reference}` —
  register an end customer under your own key, and read it back.
- `POST /manufacturer-api/v1/service-locations` and
  `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/service-locations/{reference}` — the same for that customer's sites.
- `POST /manufacturer-api/v1/equipment` and
  `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/equipment?serialNumber=…` — register one of your units at a registered
  site, keyed by its serial number, and look your units up by serial number. A serial number already
  known at another site answers `409`.
- All three registrations find-or-create only — no update, no delete, no listing — and are
  idempotent on your key (`200` + `Idempotent-Replayed: true` on a repeat); see
  [Registering your directory](#registering-your-directory).
- `GET /manufacturer-api/v1/problems` — the read-only problem catalogue, paged like the change feed →
  `{ items, nextCursor, hasMore }`, filterable by `equipmentType` and `search`; see
  [Problem catalog](#problem-catalog).

The `1.0.0-preview`, `1.1.0-preview` and `1.2.0-preview` documents published while the API was being
built are superseded by this release. Nothing that was in them was removed or narrowed. No earlier
`1.0.0` document was released to partners: this entry describes the only `1.0.0` there has ever
been.

post.description:
Registers one of your end customers in FixFlow under **your own** `reference` — the customer's id in your system — so later work orders can address it by that key alone.

`reference` is the idempotency key: the first call answers `201 Created` with a `Location` header, and every later call with the same value answers `200 OK` with the **same, unchanged** customer plus the response header `Idempotent-Replayed: true`. The body of a repeat is ignored entirely — registration never updates a stored row, because the directory belongs to the service company. Two calls that race each other still produce one mapping.

**Matching.** With `address` we look for an existing customer with the same name **and** the same `addressLine1` + ZIP — either the customer's own address or the address of one of its sites — and map your key onto it; otherwise a new customer is created from what you sent. Without `address` nothing is matched and a new customer is always created: a name alone is never enough, since two unrelated companies may share one.

There is no update, delete or list here: a registered key is read back one at a time.

example.detail: A valid API key is required.

address.zip: ZIP is required when an address is sent.

get.summary: Read one customer by your own reference
get.description:
Returns the customer your `reference` is mapped to, so you never have to store FixFlow ids.

The scope is your own mappings only: a reference you never registered, and the same value registered by another manufacturer, both answer the same `404` — the API never confirms that a directory row exists.

The resource is deliberately minimal (`id`, `reference`, `name`). Phone, email and the customer's own address stay inside FixFlow.

parameters.name: reference
parameters.description: The customer's id in your system, as you registered it (URL-encoded).

post.summary: Register a unit by its serial number
post.description:
Registers one of **your own** units at a site you have already registered, so later work orders can name the unit by its serial number alone.

`serviceLocationReference` must already be registered by you (`POST /service-locations`), otherwise the call answers `422` on that field.

`serialNumber` is **required** here — it is the unit's key, the way `reference` is a customer's. The serial number is the idempotency key, together with the site:

- no unit of yours carries it yet → the unit is created under **your** brand and the call answers `201 Created` with a `Location` header pointing at the lookup below;
- one of your units at **that same site** already carries it → `200 OK` with the **same, unchanged** unit plus `Idempotent-Replayed: true`. The body of a repeat is ignored entirely: registration never updates a stored unit;
- one of your units at a **different** site carries it → `409 Conflict`, and nothing is changed. We never move a unit between sites — ask the dispatcher.

Matching only ever looks at units of your own brand: equipment of another brand is never matched, changed or reported, even when it carries the very same serial number.

If `modelNumber` is in your model catalogue in FixFlow the unit is linked to that model; an unknown model number is kept as free text, so nothing is rejected over it. `name` is what a dispatcher sees in lists; omit it and the model number is used.

Returns your units carrying this serial number, as `{ items }`, so you never have to store FixFlow ids.

The scope is your own brand: equipment of another brand with the same serial number is never returned. Normally there is exactly one item; several mean historical duplicates in the directory, which a dispatcher can merge. An unknown serial number is an empty `items`, not a `404`.

get.description:
Returns FixFlow's catalogue of problem codes, page by page, so you can send `problemId` when you create a work order instead of describing the fault in free text only.

The catalogue belongs to the service company: it is **read-only** here, and the same entries are visible to every key — there is nothing manufacturer-specific about it. Internal accounting attributes (estimates, DNE limits, GL codes, CapEx flags) are never part of this response.

**Paging.** Entries come back in a stable order, `limit` per page (1–500, 100 by default). While `hasMore` is `true`, call again with `cursor` set to the `nextCursor` you just received; on the last page `nextCursor` is `null`. The cursor is opaque — store it verbatim and make no assumptions about its contents.

**Filters.** `equipmentType` matches the equipment type's name exactly (case-insensitive); `search` matches a substring of the problem's name or code (case-insensitive). The catalogue changes rarely, so the usual pattern is to walk it once and cache it, refreshing it on a schedule.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: The `nextCursor` of your previous page, verbatim. Omit it to start from the beginning.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: How many catalogue entries one page may carry: 1–500, 100 by default.

parameters.name: equipmentType
parameters.description: Keep only the problems of this equipment type (its exact name, case-insensitive).

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Keep only the problems whose name or code contains this text (case-insensitive).

items.name: Unit does not cool
items.description: No cooling at all, or the discharge air stays above setpoint.

  -H "X-Api-Key: $FIXFLOW_API_KEY"

post.description:
Registers one of your customer's sites under **your own** `reference` — the site's id in your system — so later work orders can address it by that key alone.

`customerReference` must already be registered by you (`POST /customers`), otherwise the call answers `422` on that field: a site cannot exist without its customer, and we never reveal that a key belongs to somebody else.

`reference` is the idempotency key, exactly as for customers: the first call answers `201 Created` with a `Location` header, a repeat answers `200 OK` with the **same, unchanged** site plus `Idempotent-Replayed: true`, and the body of a repeat is ignored entirely. Registration never updates a stored site.

**Matching.** Among that customer's existing sites we look for the same `addressLine1` + ZIP (letter case and extra spaces ignored, ZIP compared on its first five digits, so `08608` and `08608-1234` are the same place) and map your key onto it; otherwise the site is created, named `name` or — if you omit it — after the street line.

**No site id in your system?** Use any key you can rebuild from your own data for the same site every time — for example the customer id plus the site number (`CUST-99812/4`). It never has to mean anything to FixFlow; it only has to be stable.

post.description:
Submits a repair request for one of your units at an end customer's site. FixFlow matches or creates the customer, the service location and the unit itself, then opens the work order in status `New` for a dispatcher to triage.

**Address the customer and the site with your own keys.** `customer.reference` (the customer's id in your system) and `serviceLocation.reference` (the site's id) are both required, and resolution is key first: a key we have already seen leads to the very same directory row every time — even if the name or address in this request differs — and that row is never overwritten from a request. The other customer and address fields are needed only while a key is still unknown to us: `customer.name` for a new customer key, `addressLine1`, `city`, `state` and `zip` for a new site key, and `equipment.modelNumber` only when no unit of yours with that serial number is found at the site. A mapped site that belongs to a different customer answers `422`.

`externalReference` — your own claim or case number — is the idempotency key: the first call creates the work order (`201`), every later call with the same value returns that same work order unchanged (`200` with the `Idempotent-Replayed: true` header). Retrying a timed-out request is therefore always safe.

The unit always belongs to the manufacturer the key is bound to, so the work order shows up in your scope by construction; equipment of another brand is never matched or modified.

get.summary: Read a batch of work orders
get.description:
Reads up to 100 work orders in one call, addressed by FixFlow ids (`ids`), by your own references (`references`), or by both. Each parameter takes a comma-separated list and may also be repeated.

`items` carries the work orders that are yours, ordered by id. Everything else — unknown, another manufacturer's, or no longer in your scope — is echoed back under `notFound`, exactly as you asked for it, so one unknown identifier never fails the whole call.

This is the resync tool: when the change feed's cursor is lost or your copy looks stale, re-read the work orders you care about in batches of 100.

get.description:
Streams the work orders of yours that changed, so you never have to re-read the ones that did not. There are no webhooks in `v1`: this feed is how you track state.

**The loop.** Call it once without parameters — you get no items and a `nextCursor` that means "from now on". Persist that cursor, then every 30–60 seconds call again with it; each answer gives you the changed work orders plus a new cursor to persist. While `hasMore` is `true` there are already more changes waiting, so you may keep calling immediately instead of waiting for the next tick.

**Items are snapshots, not diffs.** Each item is the work order exactly as it is now, plus `changedAt` — when we last saw it change. Several changes to one work order inside one page collapse into one item.

**Be idempotent.** Delivery is at-least-once: the same snapshot can arrive twice, so apply items by id rather than counting events. For the same reason the feed deliberately lags a few seconds behind live, and a page can come back empty with a moved cursor (changes to work orders outside your scope advance it without being shown).

`cursor` is opaque — store it verbatim and make no assumptions about its contents. To backfill instead of subscribing, pass `since` with an ISO-8601 instant; `cursor` wins when you send both. If a cursor is ever lost, resync with the batch read.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: The `nextCursor` of your previous page, verbatim. Omit it to subscribe from now on.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: How many changed work orders one page may carry: 1–500, 100 by default.

parameters.name: since
parameters.description: Backfill from this ISO-8601 instant instead of subscribing from now (for example `2026-10-13T15:48:02Z`). Ignored when `cursor` is sent.

items.description: Unit shuts down after 10 minutes and reports error E-14.

cursor: The cursor is not valid. Resync with a batch read, then subscribe again.

# 1. Subscribe from now: no items, just the current nextCursor. Store it.
curl "https://<your-fixflow-host>/fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/changes" \
  -H "X-Api-Key: $FIXFLOW_API_KEY"

# 2. Every 30-60 s: pass the last nextCursor verbatim and store the new one.
#    While hasMore is true, call again straight away.
curl "https://<your-fixflow-host>/fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/changes?cursor=$CURSOR&limit=100" \
  -H "X-Api-Key: $FIXFLOW_API_KEY"

# Backfill from a moment in time instead of a cursor:
curl "https://<your-fixflow-host>/fixflow/manufacturer-api/v1/work-orders/changes?since=2026-10-01T00:00:00Z" \
  -H "X-Api-Key: $FIXFLOW_API_KEY"
